questions.q: State the approximate thickness range of the continental crust and the oceanic crust, and name the dominant rock type in each.
questions.a: Continental crust: 30–70 km thick, dominated by granitic (SIAL) rocks; Oceanic crust: 5–10 km thick, dominated by basaltic (SIMA) rocks. A wrong answer (e.g., "both are 30 km" or "oceanic crust is granitic") reveals the student has not internalised the fundamental thickness-composition dichotomy that drives isostasy and plate tectonics.

questions.q: Explain why S-waves cannot travel through the outer core, and what this tells us about its physical state.
questions.a: S-waves are shear waves requiring material rigidity (shear modulus > 0); they cannot propagate through fluids. Their absence (S-wave shadow zone) in the outer core proves it is liquid (molten iron-nickel alloy). A wrong answer (e.g., "S-waves are absorbed by heat") reveals confusion between attenuation and the fundamental physics of wave propagation in fluids vs solids.

questions.q: A P-wave travels vertically downward from the surface. At the Mohorovičić discontinuity (depth 35 km), its velocity jumps from 6.8 km/s to 8.1 km/s. Calculate the critical angle for total internal reflection of this P-wave at the Moho. (Use Snell's law: sin i / sin r = v1 / v2)
questions.a: Step 1: Identify v1 = 6.8 km/s (crust), v2 = 8.1 km/s (mantle). Step 2: Critical angle occurs when refracted ray grazes the boundary (r = 90°), so sin r = 1. Step 3: sin i_c = v1 / v2 = 6.8 / 8.1 ≈ 0.8395. Step 4: i_c = sin⁻¹(0.8395) ≈ 57.1°. A wrong answer (e.g., using v2/v1 or forgetting the inverse sine) reveals inability to apply wave physics to geological boundaries — a key skill for interpreting seismic tomography.

questions.q: Compare the Gutenberg discontinuity (core-mantle boundary) and the Lehmann discontinuity (inner-outer core boundary) in terms of: (a) depth, (b) seismic wave behaviour, (c) inferred physical change.
questions.a: (a) Gutenberg at ~2,900 km; Lehmann at ~5,150 km. (b) Gutenberg: P-wave velocity drops sharply (13.7 → 8.1 km/s), S-waves disappear; Lehmann: P-wave velocity jumps (8.1 → 11.2 km/s), S-waves remain absent. (c) Gutenberg marks solid mantle → liquid outer core (compositional + phase change); Lehmann marks liquid outer core → solid inner core (phase change only, same composition). A wrong answer conflating the two boundaries shows failure to distinguish compositional vs phase-change discontinuities.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The mantle is liquid because it convects and drives plate tectonics." Justify your answer using seismic evidence.
questions.a: The statement is **false**. The mantle is predominantly **solid** (S-waves propagate through it), but behaves as a viscous fluid over geological time due to solid-state creep (dislocation creep, diffusion creep). Seismic evidence: S-wave velocities in the mantle are 4.5–7.3 km/s — only possible in a rigid solid. Convection occurs via solid-state deformation, not melting. A student calling the mantle "liquid" confuses rheological behaviour (long-term flow) with physical state (solid vs liquid) — a classic senior-secondary error.

questions.q: Design a labelled schematic cross-section of Earth's interior (radius 6,371 km) showing: crust (continental & oceanic), mantle subdivisions, core subdivisions, and all four major discontinuities (Mohorovičić, Repetti, Gutenberg, Lehmann). Annotate each layer with: thickness, dominant composition, physical state, and P-wave velocity range.
questions.a: A good answer produces a scaled diagram (e.g., 1 cm = 500 km) with: Crust 0–35 km (cont.) / 0–7 km (ocean.), SIAL/SIMA, solid, Vp 5.5–7.0 km/s; Moho at 35/7 km; Upper Mantle to 410 km, peridotite, solid, Vp 7.8–8.5 km/s; Repetti/Transition Zone 410–660 km, wadsleyite/ringwoodite, solid, Vp 8.5–10.5 km/s; Lower Mantle 660–2,900 km, bridgmanite/ferropericlase, solid, Vp 10.5–13.7 km/s; Gutenberg at 2,900 km; Outer Core 2,900–5,150 km, Fe-Ni liquid, Vp 8.1–10.3 km/s (S-wave = 0); Lehmann at 5,150 km; Inner Core 5,150–6,371 km, Fe-Ni solid, Vp 11.2 km/s. Poor answers omit the Repetti/transition zone, mislabel states, or use uniform scaling that obscures the thin crust.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Earth's interior is ______ layered into three principal compositional zones: the Crust (thin, solid outer skin, 5–70 km thick, differentiated into granitic continental crust and basaltic oceanic crust), the Mantle (thick, predominantly solid but ductile silicate shell extending to 2,900 km depth, subdivided into upper mantle, transition zone, and lower mantle), and the Core (dense, metallic sphere of iron-nickel alloy from 2,900 km to the centre at 6,371 km, with a liquid outer core and solid inner core).

Fill in the blank: Imagine standing on the railway platform at Leh (Ladakh, 3,500 m ______) and then at Chennai beach (sea level) — the ground beneath your feet feels solid, yet the crust is only 30–50 km thick here versus 5–10 km under the Indian Ocean.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can: (1) sketch a labelled cross-section of Earth showing crust, mantle, core with correct relative thicknesses and discontinuity names (Mohorovičić, Gutenberg, Lehmann), and (2) explain how seismic wave velocity changes (P-wave/S-wave behaviour) at each boundary provide evidence for compositional and phase changes.
